1 Base class pointers and references

1.1 Our Base and Derived

base_derived.h
#ifndef BASE_DERIVED_H
#define BASE_DERIVED_H

#include <string_view>

class Base {
  protected:
    int id{};

  public:
    Base(int id) : id{id} {}
    std::string_view get_name() const { return "Base"; } // NOT virtual
};

class Derived : public Base {
  private:
    double value{};

  public:
    Derived(double value, int id) : Base{id}, value{value} {}
    std::string_view get_name() const { return "Derived"; }
    double get_value() const { return value; }
};

#endif

Nothing new here: Derived inherits from Base, and has its own get_name() that hides Base::get_name() (Chapter 14).

1.2 Pointers and references to derived objects

pointers_references_to_derived.cpp
#include "base_derived.h"
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    Derived derived{42.24, 42};
    Derived& ref{derived};
    Derived* ptr{&derived};
    std::cout << derived.get_name() << ' ' << derived.get_value() << '\n';
    std::cout << ref.get_name() << ' ' << ref.get_value() << '\n';
    std::cout << ptr->get_name() << ' ' << ptr->get_value() << '\n';
    return 0;
}
Derived 42.24
Derived 42.24
Derived 42.24

Still nothing new: a Derived reference or pointer behaves just like the Derived object itself.

1.3 A base reference to a derived object

base_pointers_references_to_derived.cpp
#include "base_derived.h"
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    Derived derived{42.24, 42};
    Base& base_ref{derived};  // a Base reference to a Derived object
    Base* base_ptr{&derived}; // a Base pointer to a Derived object
    std::cout << derived.get_name() << '\n';
    std::cout << base_ref.get_name() << '\n';  // which get_name()?
    std::cout << base_ptr->get_name() << '\n'; // which get_name()?
    // base_ref.get_value(); // error: a Base has no get_value()
    return 0;
}
Derived
Base
Base

A Derived object has a Base part, so a Base reference or pointer can refer to it. But look at what it calls!

1.4 A base reference sees only the base part

Derived::get_name() hides Base::get_name() for Derived objects. But through a Base reference or pointer, the compiler only knows about the Base part, so it calls Base::get_name().

1.5 Why would we want that?

Suppose we have cats, dogs and tigers, and want to report what each one says:

void report(const Cat& cat) {
    std::cout << cat.get_name() << " says " << cat.speak() << '\n';
}
void report(const Dog& dog) {
    std::cout << dog.get_name() << " says " << dog.speak() << '\n';
}
void report(const Tiger& tiger) {
    std::cout << tiger.get_name() << " says " << tiger.speak() << '\n';
}

A zoo with 100 kinds of animal means 100 copies of the same function. We’d much rather write one:

void report(const Animal& animal) {
    std::cout << animal.get_name() << " says " << animal.speak() << '\n';
}

1.6 Couldn’t a template do it?

template <typename T>
void report(const T& animal) {
    std::cout << animal.get_name() << " says " << animal.speak() << '\n';
}

It works, but:

  • nothing says T must be an animal: report(42) gives a long, confusing template error;
  • each type gets its own instance, decided at compile time. A template can’t handle a collection of mixed animals whose types are only known when the program runs.

1.7 Our animals

animals_nonvirtual.h
#ifndef ANIMALS_NONVIRTUAL_H
#define ANIMALS_NONVIRTUAL_H

#include <string>
#include <string_view>
class Animal {
  protected:
    std::string name{};
    Animal(std::string_view name) : name{name} {}

  public:
    std::string_view get_name() const { return name; }
    std::string_view speak() const { return "???"; }
};
class Cat : public Animal {
  public:
    Cat(std::string_view name) : Animal{name} {}
    std::string_view speak() const { return "Meow"; }
};
class Dog : public Animal {
  public:
    Dog(std::string_view name) : Animal{name} {}
    std::string_view speak() const { return "Woof"; }
};
#endif

The constructor of Animal is protected, so nobody can create a plain Animal: only cats and dogs.

std::string_view is a cheap, read-only view of some text (Chapter 04).

1.8 One array per kind of animal

different_animal_arrays.cpp
#include "animals_nonvirtual.h"
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    // Without a common type, every kind of animal needs its own array...
    const Cat cats[]{Cat{"Fred"}, Cat{"Misty"}, Cat{"Zeke"}};
    const Dog dogs[]{Dog{"Garbo"}, Dog{"Pooky"}, Dog{"Truffle"}};

    for (const auto& cat : cats) { // ...and its own loop
        std::cout << cat.get_name() << " says " << cat.speak() << '\n';
    }
    for (const auto& dog : dogs) {
        std::cout << dog.get_name() << " says " << dog.speak() << '\n';
    }
    return 0;
}
Fred says Meow
Misty says Meow
Zeke says Meow
Garbo says Woof
Pooky says Woof
Truffle says Woof

An array holds objects of one type, so each kind of animal needs its own array and its own loop. With 100 kinds, that’s 100 arrays.

1.9 One vector of Animal pointers?

animal_array.cpp
#include "animals_nonvirtual.h"
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    const Cat fred{"Fred"};
    const Cat misty{"Misty"};
    const Dog garbo{"Garbo"};
    const Dog pooky{"Pooky"};

    // One vector of Animal pointers holds cats AND dogs
    const std::vector<const Animal*> animals{&fred, &garbo, &misty, &pooky};

    for (const Animal* animal : animals) {
        std::cout << animal->get_name() << " says " << animal->speak() << '\n';
    }
    return 0;
}
Fred says ???
Garbo says ???
Misty says ???
Pooky says ???

Base pointers let one vector hold every kind of animal. But they all say ???: each call goes to Animal::speak(). We need virtual functions.

2 Virtual functions

2.1 Virtual functions

A virtual function is a member function that, when called through a base pointer or reference, resolves to the most-derived version for the actual object.

  • Put virtual in front of the function in the base class.
  • A function in a derived class with the same signature and return type overrides it, and is called an override. Mark it override.

2.2 A first virtual function

virtual_function_example.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string_view>

class Base {
  public:
    virtual std::string_view get_name() const { return "Base"; } // virtual!
};
class Derived : public Base {
  public:
    std::string_view get_name() const override { return "Derived"; }
};

int main() {
    Derived derived{};
    Base& base_ref{derived};
    std::cout << "base_ref is a " << base_ref.get_name() << '\n';
    return 0;
}
base_ref is a Derived

One word, virtual, and the call through base_ref now reaches Derived::get_name().

2.3 Virtual functions in a chain

virtual_function_inheritance_chain.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string_view>

class A {
  public:
    virtual std::string_view get_name() const { return "A"; }
};
class B : public A {
  public:
    std::string_view get_name() const override { return "B"; }
};
class C : public B {
  public:
    std::string_view get_name() const override { return "C"; }
};
class D : public C {
  public:
    std::string_view get_name() const override { return "D"; }
};

int main() {
    C c{};
    A& base_ref{c};
    std::cout << "base_ref is a " << base_ref.get_name() << '\n';
    return 0;
}
base_ref is a C

base_ref refers to a C, so C::get_name() is called: the most-derived version for the actual object. D doesn’t come into it, because the object isn’t a D.

2.4 The animals, with a virtual speak()

animals.h
#ifndef ANIMALS_H
#define ANIMALS_H

#include <string>
#include <string_view>
class Animal {
  protected:
    std::string name{};
    Animal(std::string_view name) : name{name} {}

  public:
    virtual ~Animal() = default; // a virtual destructor: see later
    std::string_view get_name() const { return name; }
    virtual std::string_view speak() const { return "???"; } // virtual!
};
class Cat : public Animal {
  public:
    Cat(std::string_view name) : Animal{name} {}
    std::string_view speak() const override { return "Meow"; }
};
class Dog : public Animal {
  public:
    Dog(std::string_view name) : Animal{name} {}
    std::string_view speak() const override { return "Woof"; }
};
#endif

Two changes from before:

  • virtual in front of Animal::speak();
  • override after each derived speak().

(And a virtual destructor, explained later today.)

2.5 Now every animal speaks for itself

animals_with_virtual.cpp
#include "animals.h" // the same classes, with a virtual speak()
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

void report(const Animal& animal) {
    std::cout << animal.get_name() << " says " << animal.speak() << '\n';
}

int main() {
    report(Cat{"Felix"});
    report(Dog{"Rex"});

    const Cat fred{"Fred"};
    const Dog garbo{"Garbo"};
    const std::vector<const Animal*> animals{&fred, &garbo};
    for (const Animal* animal : animals) {
        report(*animal);
    }
    return 0;
}
Felix says Meow
Rex says Woof
Fred says Meow
Garbo says Woof

The same report() function as before (animals_without_virtual.cpp, where everyone said ???). Only the header changed.

2.6 Behind the scenes (read at home)

Every object of a class with virtual functions carries a hidden pointer to its class’s virtual table, which lists the right function for each virtual call. Following it costs a tiny bit of time, which is why C++ functions aren’t virtual unless you ask.

2.7 Polymorphism

Polymorphism means one name with many forms, chosen according to the types involved:

  • Compile-time polymorphism is resolved by the compiler: function overloading (Chapter 05) and templates (Chapter 06).
  • Run-time polymorphism is resolved while the program runs: virtual functions.
ImportantKey idea

With virtual functions, code written for the base class (like report(const Animal&)) automatically does the right thing for every derived class, even ones written years later.

2.8 The rules of overriding

  • An override needs exactly the same signature as the base function (parameter types and const), and is itself virtual.
  • The return types must match too:
virtual_return_type_mismatch.cpp
class Base {
  public:
    virtual int get_value() const { return 5; }
};
class Derived : public Base {
  public:
    double get_value() const { return 6.78; } // error: different return type
};

int main() {
    Derived derived{};
    return 0;
}
error: conflicting return type specified for 'virtual double Derived::get_value() const'

3 The override and final specifiers

3.1 Overrides that don’t override

not_use_override_specifier.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string_view>

class A {
  public:
    virtual std::string_view get_name_1(int) const { return "A"; }
    virtual std::string_view get_name_2(int) const { return "A"; }
};
class B : public A {
  public:
    // Look closely: neither of these overrides anything!
    virtual std::string_view get_name_1(short) const { return "B"; }
    virtual std::string_view get_name_2(int) { return "B"; } // not const
};

int main() {
    B b{};
    A& base_ref{b};
    std::cout << base_ref.get_name_1(1) << '\n';
    std::cout << base_ref.get_name_2(2) << '\n';
    return 0;
}
A
A

Both calls go to A. B::get_name_1(short) takes a short, not an int, and B::get_name_2 isn’t const: neither is an override. Only -Wall hints at it: “… was hidden”.

3.2 override turns the bug into an error

use_override_specifier.cpp
#include <string_view>
class A {
  public:
    virtual std::string_view get_name_1(int) const { return "A"; }
    virtual std::string_view get_name_2(int) const { return "A"; }
    virtual std::string_view get_name_3(int) const { return "A"; }
};
class B : public A {
  public:
    std::string_view get_name_1(short) const override { return "B"; } // error
    std::string_view get_name_2(int) override { return "B"; }         // error
    std::string_view get_name_3(int) const override { return "B"; }   // fine
};

int main() {
    B b{};
    return 0;
}
error: 'B::get_name_1(short int) const' marked 'override', but does not override
error: 'B::get_name_2(int)' marked 'override', but does not override
TipBest practice

Write virtual only in the base class, and override on every override.

3.3 The final specifier

final stops a function from being overridden any further:

final_specifier_example.cpp
#include <string_view>
class A {
  public:
    virtual std::string_view get_name() const { return "A"; }
};
class B : public A {
  public:
    std::string_view get_name() const override final { return "B"; }
};
class C : public B {
  public:
    std::string_view get_name() const override { return "C"; } // error
};

int main() {
    C c{};
    return 0;
}
error: virtual function 'virtual std::string_view C::get_name() const' overriding final function

And class B final : public A would stop anyone deriving from B at all.

4 Slicing and virtual destructors

4.1 Object slicing

object_slicing.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string_view>

class Base {
  public:
    virtual ~Base() = default;
    virtual std::string_view get_name() const { return "Base"; }
};
class Derived : public Base {
  public:
    std::string_view get_name() const override { return "Derived"; }
};

int main() {
    Derived derived{};
    Base& ref{derived}; // a reference: refers to the whole Derived
    Base copy{derived}; // a copy: only the Base part is copied!
    std::cout << "ref is a " << ref.get_name() << '\n';
    std::cout << "copy is a " << copy.get_name() << '\n';
    return 0;
}
ref is a Derived
copy is a Base

A reference refers to the whole Derived. A copy into a Base keeps only the Base part: the rest is sliced off.

4.2 What slicing means in practice

  • A std::vector<Animal> would slice every cat and dog into a plain Animal. That’s why we used std::vector<const Animal*>.
  • Pass polymorphic objects by reference or pointer, never by value.

4.3 Deleting through a base pointer

virtual_destructor.cpp
#include <iostream>

class Base {
  public:
    ~Base() { std::cout << "~Base()\n"; } // NOT virtual
    virtual void hello() const { std::cout << "Hello from Base\n"; }
};
class Derived : public Base {
  public:
    ~Derived() { std::cout << "~Derived()\n"; } // cleans up Derived's part
};

int main() {
    Base* ptr{new Derived{}}; // a Base pointer to a heap Derived
    delete ptr;               // which destructors run?
    return 0;
}
$ g++ -Wall virtual_destructor.cpp
warning: deleting object of polymorphic class type 'Base' which has non-virtual destructor might cause undefined behavior
$ ./a.out
~Base()

~Derived() never ran! If Derived owned memory, it would leak.

4.4 Virtual destructors

virtual_destructor_fixed.cpp
#include <iostream>

class Base {
  public:
    virtual ~Base() { std::cout << "~Base()\n"; } // virtual now
    virtual void hello() const { std::cout << "Hello from Base\n"; }
};
class Derived : public Base {
  public:
    ~Derived() override { std::cout << "~Derived()\n"; }
};

int main() {
    Base* ptr{new Derived{}};
    delete ptr;
    return 0;
}
~Derived()
~Base()

With a virtual destructor, delete ptr calls the destructor of the actual object, then the base destructors in turn (Chapter 14).

TipBest practice

A class meant to be a base class, especially one with virtual functions, should have a virtual destructor: virtual ~Base() = default;

5 Pure virtual functions and abstract classes

5.1 Forgetting to override

virtual_function_forget_redefine.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>

class Animal {
  protected:
    std::string name{};
    Animal(std::string_view name) : name{name} {}

  public:
    virtual ~Animal() = default;
    std::string_view get_name() const { return name; }
    virtual std::string_view speak() const { return "???"; }
};
class Cow : public Animal {
  public:
    Cow(std::string_view name) : Animal{name} {}
    // We forgot to override speak()!
};

int main() {
    Cow cow{"Betsy"};
    std::cout << cow.get_name() << " says " << cow.speak() << '\n';
    return 0;
}
Betsy says ???

We forgot Cow::speak(), so Animal::speak() quietly took over. No error, no warning: just a wrong answer.

5.2 Pure virtual functions

A pure virtual function has no body in the base class; it’s marked = 0:

virtual std::string_view speak() const = 0; // "every animal MUST say something"
  • A class with at least one pure virtual function is an abstract base class: you can’t create objects of it.
  • A derived class must override every pure virtual function, or it’s abstract too.
  • Only virtual functions can be pure: int do_something() = 0; is a compile error.

So: what does an Animal say? There’s no sensible default, and now we don’t have to invent one.

5.3 Forgetting now fails to compile

pure_virtual_function_forget_redefine.cpp
#include <string>
#include <string_view>
class Animal { // an abstract base class
  protected:
    std::string name{};
    Animal(std::string_view name) : name{name} {}

  public:
    virtual ~Animal() = default;
    std::string_view get_name() const { return name; }
    virtual std::string_view speak() const = 0; // pure virtual
};
class Cow : public Animal {
  public:
    Cow(std::string_view name) : Animal{name} {}
    // We forgot to override speak()... again!
};

int main() {
    Cow cow{"Betsy"}; // error: Cow is abstract too
    return 0;
}
error: cannot declare variable 'cow' to be of abstract type 'Cow'

A silent wrong answer is now a compile error: much better!

5.4 …and remembering works

pure_virtual_function_remember_redefine.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>

class Animal { // an abstract base class
  protected:
    std::string name{};
    Animal(std::string_view name) : name{name} {}

  public:
    virtual ~Animal() = default;
    std::string_view get_name() const { return name; }
    virtual std::string_view speak() const = 0; // pure virtual
};
class Cow : public Animal {
  public:
    Cow(std::string_view name) : Animal{name} {}
    std::string_view speak() const override { return "Moo"; } // now we must
};

int main() {
    Cow cow{"Betsy"};
    std::cout << cow.get_name() << " says " << cow.speak() << '\n';
    return 0;
}
Betsy says Moo

5.5 Interface classes

An interface class has no member variables, and only pure virtual functions. It defines what derived classes must be able to do, and leaves how entirely to them. Interface names often start with I:

class IErrorLog {
  public:
    virtual ~IErrorLog() = default; // so deleting through IErrorLog* is safe
    virtual bool open_log(std::string_view filename) = 0;
    virtual bool write_error(std::string_view message) = 0;
    virtual bool close_log() = 0;
};

Code that writes errors only needs an IErrorLog&. Whether errors go to a file, the screen or a database is decided by whichever class implements the interface.

5.6 Putting it all together: shapes

The Shape promised in Chapter 10, one class per header (Chapter 14):

shape.h
#ifndef SHAPE_H
#define SHAPE_H

#include <string_view>

class Shape { // an abstract base class: what every shape must provide
  public:
    virtual ~Shape() = default;
    virtual double area() const = 0;
    virtual std::string_view name() const = 0;
};

#endif

An abstract base class with a virtual destructor: it only says what every shape must be able to do.

5.7 A circle (and a rectangle)

circle.h
#ifndef CIRCLE_H
#define CIRCLE_H

#include "shape.h"
#include <numbers> // std::numbers::pi (Chapter 04)

class Circle : public Shape {
  private:
    double radius{};

  public:
    Circle(double radius) : radius{radius} {}
    double area() const override { return std::numbers::pi * radius * radius; }
    std::string_view name() const override { return "circle"; }
};

#endif

rectangle.h is the same idea, with a width and a height.

5.8 Every shape, in one loop

shapes.cpp
#include "circle.h"
#include "rectangle.h"
#include <iostream>
#include <memory> // std::unique_ptr (Chapter 09)
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Shape>> shapes{};
    shapes.push_back(std::make_unique<Circle>(1.0));
    shapes.push_back(std::make_unique<Rectangle>(2.0, 3.0));

    for (const auto& shape : shapes) { // one loop, every kind of shape
        std::cout << shape->name() << ": area " << shape->area() << '\n';
    }
    return 0;
} // the unique_ptrs delete the shapes, through ~Shape(): virtual!
circle: area 3.14159
rectangle: area 6

Abstract base class, overrides, a virtual destructor, and std::unique_ptr (Chapter 09) doing the delete: everything from today, working together.

6 Wrapping up

6.1 Summary

  • A base pointer or reference can refer to a derived object, but only sees the base part.
  • A virtual function call goes to the most-derived override for the actual object: run-time polymorphism.
  • Write virtual in the base class and override on every override; final stops further overriding.
  • Copying a derived object into a base object slices it: pass polymorphic objects by reference or pointer.
  • Give base classes a virtual destructor.
  • A pure virtual function (= 0) makes a class abstract; derived classes must override it. An interface is a class of pure virtual functions only.
